quote: Using records created by, and for, the Female Sanitary Inspectors (FSIs) in Bradford c. 1900–1912, this case study finds no shortage of reports describing distressing economic and social conditions.
The case study encourages a broader re-evaluation of histories of mental health care in so far as they discuss relationships to poverty and relationships between service-providers and serviceusers.

Mental health and mental deficiency were fashionable topics and staff (and their professional leaders) hoped to bolster their professional credentials by demonstrating relevant, even unique, expertise.
However, such was the stigma of mental illness that FSIs do not appear to have discussed mental health/ill-health directly with the people they visited.

value: The literature is almost silent on how contemporaries linked poverty and mental health.
quote: The literature is, for example, almost totally silent on the relationship that contemporary actors drew between poverty and mental health.

value: Mental health and well-being emerged over time as distinct concerns in the reports.
quote: Initially, FSI discussions centred on immediate threats to physical health, but over time mental health and well-being emerged as distinct concerns.

value: The staff's own well-being became a persistent concern.
quote: Interestingly, the well-being of the staff emerges as a persistent and even over-riding concern as sanitary inspection was combined with, and then increasingly displaced by, health visiting duties.

value: Staff labelled individuals mentally deficient with no evidence of official involvement.
quote: Staff confidently attached the label to various individuals whom they encountered, although there is no evidence that any of these people were known to authorities concerned with mental health and/or mental deficiency.

value: Conflating mental health with emergencies drew attention from commoner, milder problems.
quote: The unhelpful conflation of mental health issues with mental health emergencies, dangerous people, and risks to staff arguably detracted attention away from the less severe, but more common, mental health problems that the FSIs were likely to encounter.

value: Slum dwellers with mental health problems were treated as a class apart.
quote: Those slum dwellers who did exhibit mental health problems (and more particularly mental deficiency) were regarded as a different problem, even a class apart.

value: Slum dwellers sought the inspectors' help in mental health crises; officers were the reluctant party.
quote: Yet, there is ample evidence that, when confronted with mental health crises, slum dwellers actively sought the assistance of FSIs. In, fact in these scenarios, it was most often the officer rather than the client who was reluctant to proceed.

value: Most poverty was explained by low wages and inadequate resources.
quote: The Bradford FSIs, caught in the ideological contradictions already discussed, explained most of the poverty they witnessed in terms of low wages and inadequate resources, but also highlighted a distinct subset of cases where something very different was believed to be going on.

value: The quest for respectability conflicted with health and hygiene messages.
quote: The problem was that in overcrowded homes and districts, offering a minimum of privacy, the quest for respectability often directly conflicted with health and hygiene messages.
